claim: Bacterial pneumonia in neonates causes significant morbidity and mortality when compared to other childhood age groups.
source: Bacterial pneumonia in neonates can cause significant morbidity and mortality when compared to other childhood age groups.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that draws from established medical knowledge about neonatal pneumonia outcomes.

claim: E. coli challenge resulted in rapid and significant increases in neutrophils in the lungs of both neonates and juveniles.
source: E. coli challenge resulted in rapid and significant increases in neutrophils, monocytes, and γδT cells, along with significant decreases in dendritic cells and alveolar macrophages in the lungs of both neonates and juveniles.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data presented in Figure 1 showing neutrophil percentages at different time points.

claim: E. coli challenge resulted in rapid and significant increases in monocytes in the lungs of both neonates and juveniles.
source: E. coli challenge resulted in rapid and significant increases in neutrophils, monocytes, and γδT cells, along with significant decreases in dendritic cells and alveolar macrophages in the lungs of both neonates and juveniles.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data presented in Figure 2 showing monocyte dynamics.

claim: E. coli challenge resulted in rapid and significant increases in γδT cells in the lungs of both neonates and juveniles.
source: E. coli challenge resulted in rapid and significant increases in neutrophils, monocytes, and γδT cells, along with significant decreases in dendritic cells and alveolar macrophages in the lungs of both neonates and juveniles.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data presented in Figure 1 showing γδT cell percentages.

claim: E. coli challenge resulted in significant decreases in dendritic cells in the lungs of both neonates and juveniles.
source: E. coli challenge resulted in rapid and significant increases in neutrophils, monocytes, and γδT cells, along with significant decreases in dendritic cells and alveolar macrophages in the lungs of both neonates and juveniles.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data presented in Figure 2 showing dendritic cell dynamics.

claim: E. coli challenge resulted in significant decreases in alveolar macrophages in the lungs of both neonates and juveniles.
source: E. coli challenge resulted in rapid and significant increases in neutrophils, monocytes, and γδT cells, along with significant decreases in dendritic cells and alveolar macrophages in the lungs of both neonates and juveniles.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data presented in Figures 2 and 3A showing alveolar macrophage dynamics.

claim: E. coli-challenged juvenile lungs had significant increases in interstitial macrophages that were not observed in neonatal lungs.
source: E. coli-challenged juvenile lung had significant increases in interstitial macrophages and recruited monocytes that were not observed in neonatal lungs.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data presented in Figures 2 and 3B showing interstitial macrophage dynamics.

claim: E. coli-challenged juvenile lungs had significant increases in recruited monocytes that were not observed in neonatal lungs.
source: E. coli-challenged juvenile lung had significant increases in interstitial macrophages and recruited monocytes that were not observed in neonatal lungs.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data presented in Figure 2 showing monocyte dynamics.

claim: Expression of IFNγ-responsive genes was positively correlated with the levels and dynamics of MHCII-expressing innate cells in neonatal and juvenile lungs.
source: Expression of IFNγ-responsive genes was positively correlated with the levels and dynamics of MHCII-expressing innate cells in neonatal and juvenile lungs.
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data presented in Figure 6 showing gene expression patterns.

claim: Several facets of immune responsiveness in wild-type neonates were recapitulated in juvenile MHCII−/− juveniles.
source: Several facets of immune responsiveness in the wild-type neonates were recapitulated in juvenile MHCII−/− juveniles.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative flow cytometry and gene expression data presented in Figures 4, 5, and 6.

claim: Children in the youngest cohorts have a higher likelihood of infection-induced severe disease, respiratory impairment, and death from pneumonia.
source: Because it takes time to accrue sufficient exposure to microbial antigens, children in the youngest cohorts have a higher likelihood of infection-induced severe disease, respiratory impairment, and death from pneumonia (Heron, 2019; Troeger et al., 2018; Ely and Driscoll, 2019; Chan et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to epidemiological studies.

claim: Most alveolar growth occurs during the first 2 years of life.
source: This period of relative vulnerability to respiratory pathogens corresponds to a time of rapid alveolar growth; with most of this growth occurring during the first 2 years of life (Thurlbeck, 1982).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a developmental biology study.

claim: Growth in the lung is accompanied by Th2-mediated tissue remodeling.
source: Growth in the lung is accompanied by Th2-mediated tissue remodeling (Roux et al., 2011; Torow et al., 2017) that can be easily disrupted by Th1 and Th17 inflammation induced by microbial challenges.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to immunological studies.

claim: Th2-mediated tissue remodeling can be easily disrupted by Th1 and Th17 inflammation induced by microbial challenges.
source: Growth in the lung is accompanied by Th2-mediated tissue remodeling (Roux et al., 2011; Torow et al., 2017) that can be easily disrupted by Th1 and Th17 inflammation induced by microbial challenges.
evidence: This claim is based on logical inference from cited immunological studies about immune response interactions.

claim: E. coli is a pathogen commonly associated with human neonatal pneumonia.
source: In this study, we sought to understand age-related differences in the cellular and molecular responses during the acute phase of the response induced by challenge with live Escherichia coli, a pathogen commonly associated with human neonatal pneumonia (Chisti et al., 2009; Duraes et al., 2016; Green and Kolberg, 2016; Wang et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: The dose of 2.4 × 10^6 CFUs of E. coli reproducibly achieved >90% survival in both neonatal and juvenile age groups.
source: At this challenge level, we reproducibly achieved >90% survival in both age groups (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), while causing demonstrable inflammation and tissue damage (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival curve data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The dose of 2.4 × 10^6 CFUs of E. coli caused demonstrable inflammation and tissue damage in both neonatal and juvenile mice.
source: At this challenge level, we reproducibly achieved >90% survival in both age groups (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), while causing demonstrable inflammation and tissue damage (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological images shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: In neonates, E. coli exposure resulted in a rapid increase in neutrophil trafficking to the lungs that persisted through 72 hr post-E. coli challenge.
source: In neonates, E. coli exposure resulted in a rapid increase in neutrophil trafficking to the lungs that persisted through 72 hr PEC (Figure 1; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Neutrophils trafficked to the lungs of juvenile mice early after E. coli challenge but dropped to control levels by 72 hr post-E. coli challenge.
source: In contrast, while neutrophils also trafficked to the lungs of juvenile mice early, they dropped to control levels by 72 hr PEC.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1.

claim: There was a trend in both neonatal and juvenile age groups for an increase in γδT cells at the later time points after E. coli challenge.
source: Although the proportions of CD4 T and B cells did not significantly change during the early response in neonates and juveniles, there was a trend in both age groups for an increase in γδT cells at the later time points (Figure 1; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The proportions of CD4 T and B cells did not significantly change during the early response to E. coli in neonates and juveniles.
source: Although the proportions of CD4 T and B cells did not significantly change during the early response in neonates and juveniles, there was a trend in both age groups for an increase in γδT cells at the later time points (Figure 1; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1.

claim: In neonatal lungs, live E. coli challenge resulted in early and sustained drops in the proportion of dendritic cells.
source: In the lungs of neonates, while live E. coli challenge resulted in early and sustained drops in the proportion of dendritic cells (Figure 2) and alveolar macrophages (Figures 2 and 3A), the numbers of these two mononuclear cell populations were elevated through 72 hr PEC (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2.

claim: In neonatal lungs, live E. coli challenge resulted in early and sustained drops in the proportion of alveolar macrophages.
source: In the lungs of neonates, while live E. coli challenge resulted in early and sustained drops in the proportion of dendritic cells (Figure 2) and alveolar macrophages (Figures 2 and 3A), the numbers of these two mononuclear cell populations were elevated through 72 hr PEC (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figures 2 and 3A.

claim: In neonatal lungs, the numbers of dendritic cells and alveolar macrophages were elevated through 72 hr post-E. coli challenge.
source: In the lungs of neonates, while live E. coli challenge resulted in early and sustained drops in the proportion of dendritic cells (Figure 2) and alveolar macrophages (Figures 2 and 3A), the numbers of these two mononuclear cell populations were elevated through 72 hr PEC (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The different trends for cell number and cell proportions are likely due to the large influx of neutrophils into the lungs.
source: The different trends for the cell number and cell proportions are likely due to the large influx of neutrophils into the lungs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is based on logical inference from the observed data patterns.

claim: There was a rapid drop in the proportion of dendritic cells and alveolar macrophages in the lungs of juveniles after E. coli challenge.
source: There was also a rapid drop in the proportion of dendritic cells and alveolar macrophages in the lungs of juveniles, but in contrast to neonates, these cells recovered to control levels by 72 hr PEC, albeit with a distinct alteration in surface expression of F4/80 and SiglecF, suggesting an altered activation status (Figures 2 and 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figures 2 and 3A.

claim: In juvenile lungs, dendritic cells and alveolar macrophages recovered to control levels by 72 hr post-E. coli challenge.
source: There was also a rapid drop in the proportion of dendritic cells and alveolar macrophages in the lungs of juveniles, but in contrast to neonates, these cells recovered to control levels by 72 hr PEC, albeit with a distinct alteration in surface expression of F4/80 and SiglecF, suggesting an altered activation status (Figures 2 and 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figures 2 and 3A.

claim: Alveolar macrophages in juvenile lungs showed a distinct alteration in surface expression of F4/80 and SiglecF after E. coli challenge, suggesting an altered activation status.
source: There was also a rapid drop in the proportion of dendritic cells and alveolar macrophages in the lungs of juveniles, but in contrast to neonates, these cells recovered to control levels by 72 hr PEC, albeit with a distinct alteration in surface expression of F4/80 and SiglecF, suggesting an altered activation status (Figures 2 and 3A).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from flow cytometry data showing altered surface marker expression in Figure 3A.

claim: Lungs from E. coli-challenged juveniles displayed a sustained expansion of the interstitial macrophage compartment.
source: While the lungs from E. coli-challenged juveniles displayed a sustained expansion of the interstitial macrophage compartment, there was no change to the constitutively low levels of this cell population in neonatal lungs (Figures 2 and 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figures 2 and 3B.

claim: There was no change to the constitutively low levels of interstitial macrophages in neonatal lungs after E. coli challenge.
source: While the lungs from E. coli-challenged juveniles displayed a sustained expansion of the interstitial macrophage compartment, there was no change to the constitutively low levels of this cell population in neonatal lungs (Figures 2 and 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figures 2 and 3B.

claim: Recruited Ly6chi monocytes contributed to the expansion of the interstitial macrophage compartment in juveniles in response to E. coli challenge.
source: The dynamic changes in the levels of Ly6c expression on the surface of CD45+F4/80+CD11b+SiglecF−MHCII+ cells, a heterogenous population that included interstitial macrophages (Figure 3B), suggest that recruited Ly6chi monocytes contributed to the expansion of this compartment in juveniles in response to E. coli challenge as reported by others (Chakarov et al., 2019; Schyns et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from flow cytometry data in Figure 3B and supported by citations.

claim: The putative recruited monocyte-to-interstitial macrophage transition after E. coli challenge was not observed in neonatal lungs.
source: This putative recruited monocyte-to-interstitial macrophage transition after E. coli challenge was not observed in the neonatal lungs.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the flow cytometry data showing lack of interstitial macrophage expansion in neonates.

claim: There was a significant increase in monocytes in juvenile lungs by 48 hr post-E. coli challenge.
source: Although there was a significant increase in monocytes in the juvenile lungs by 48 hr PEC, the proportion of monocytes in the neonatal lungs did not significantly change (Figure 2) despite significant changes in numbers (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The proportion of monocytes in neonatal lungs did not significantly change after E. coli challenge despite significant changes in numbers.
source: Although there was a significant increase in monocytes in the juvenile lungs by 48 hr PEC, the proportion of monocytes in the neonatal lungs did not significantly change (Figure 2) despite significant changes in numbers (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The MHCII−/− neonates and juveniles had 80–85% survival at 72 hr after challenge with 2.4 × 10^6 CFUs of E. coli.
source: The MHCII−/− neonates and juveniles had 80–85% survival at the 72 hr mark after the challenge with 2.4 × 106 CFUs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival curve data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Notable levels of cellular infiltrates were observed in the lungs of MHCII−/− neonates and juveniles in response to E. coli challenge.
source: In the lungs of MHCII−/− neonates and juvenile there were notable levels of cellular infiltrates observed, in response to E. coli challenge (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological images shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The total CD45+ cell count significantly increased in both WT neonatal and WT juvenile lungs in response to E. coli challenge.
source: The total CD45+ cell count significantly increased in both WT neonatal and WT juvenile lungs in response to E. coli challenge, with a substantively larger growth in the juvenile lungs (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The increase in total CD45+ cells in response to E. coli challenge was substantively larger in juvenile lungs compared to neonatal lungs.
source: The total CD45+ cell count significantly increased in both WT neonatal and WT juvenile lungs in response to E. coli challenge, with a substantively larger growth in the juvenile lungs (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5.

claim: CD45+ cell dynamics was muted in the lungs from MHCII−/− animals compared to WT animals.
source: In contrast, CD45+ cell dynamics was muted in the lungs from MHCII−/− animals.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5.

claim: MHCII−/− neonates and juveniles had an increase in the percentages and numbers of neutrophils at 48 hr post-E. coli challenge.
source: As observed in WT animals, MHCII−/− neonates and juveniles had an increase in the percentages and numbers of neutrophils at 48 hr PEC (Figures 1, 4 and 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figures 1, 4, and 5.

claim: γδT cells showed a proportional increase in MHCII−/− lungs after E. coli challenge.
source: Although γδT cells showed a proportional increase in the MHCII−/− lungs (Figure 4), this was not reflected in an increase in γδT cell numbers, as seen in the WT animals (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The proportional increase in γδT cells in MHCII−/− lungs was not reflected in an increase in γδT cell numbers.
source: Although γδT cells showed a proportional increase in the MHCII−/− lungs (Figure 4), this was not reflected in an increase in γδT cell numbers, as seen in the WT animals (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: CD4 T cells were minimal in MHCII−/− lungs from both age groups.
source: CD4 T cells were minimal in MHCII−/− lungs from both age groups.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: The proportions and numbers of B cells, dendritic cells, and monocytes in MHCII−/− neonatal and juvenile lungs at 48 hr post-E. coli challenge were similar to those found in WT animals.
source: The proportions and numbers of B cells, dendritic cells, and monocytes found in MHCII−/− neonatal and juvenile lungs at 48 hr PEC were similar to those found in WT animals (Figures 1, 2, 4 and 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figures 1, 2, 4, and 5.

claim: The alveolar macrophage response to E. coli challenge remained blunted in both MHCII−/− age groups at 48 hr post-E. coli challenge compared to WT lungs.
source: Interestingly, compared to the response in WT lungs, the alveolar macrophage response to E. coli challenge remained blunted in both MHCII−/− age groups at 48 hr, PEC.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: The proportions of interstitial macrophages and monocytes were modestly higher in both neonatal and juvenile MHCII−/− lungs.
source: Although the proportions of interstitial macrophages and monocytes were modestly higher in both neonatal and juvenile MHCII−/− lungs (Figure 4), these proportional increases corresponded to significant increases in cell numbers (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The proportional increases in interstitial macrophages and monocytes in MHCII−/− lungs corresponded to significant increases in cell numbers.
source: Although the proportions of interstitial macrophages and monocytes were modestly higher in both neonatal and juvenile MHCII−/− lungs (Figure 4), these proportional increases corresponded to significant increases in cell numbers (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5.

claim: MHCII signaling contributes to the early regulation of proliferation and/or activation of key innate cells in the neonatal lung environment.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that MHCII signaling contributes to the early regulation of proliferation and/or activation of key innate cells in the neonatal lung environment.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the comparative data between WT and MHCII−/− animals.

claim: TNF and IL-6 are induced early downstream of signaling of pattern recognition receptors.
source: The proinflammatory cytokines TNF and IL-6 are induced early downstream of signaling of pattern recognition receptors (Li and Wu, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to an immunology study.

claim: tnf and Il6 transcription was increased in neonatal and juvenile lungs from both WT and MHCII−/− animals after E. coli challenge.
source: While tnf and Il6 transcription was increased in neonatal and juvenile lungs from both WT and MHC−/− animals, WT juvenile lungs had heightened responsiveness at 24 and 48 hr, PEC compared to the other groups (Figure 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6.

claim: WT juvenile lungs had heightened tnf and Il6 transcription responsiveness at 24 and 48 hr post-E. coli challenge compared to other groups.
source: While tnf and Il6 transcription was increased in neonatal and juvenile lungs from both WT and MHC−/− animals, WT juvenile lungs had heightened responsiveness at 24 and 48 hr, PEC compared to the other groups (Figure 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6.

claim: WT juvenile lungs had the highest fold increase in Ciita expression at 24 and 48 hr post-E. coli challenge.
source: As predicted from the enhanced numbers of MHCII-positive cells (Figure 2), the WT juvenile lungs had the highest fold increase in Ciita expression at 24 and 48 hr, PEC while the lungs from WT neonates and MHCII−/− animals had minimal expression of lung Ciita at any time point (Figure 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The lungs from WT neonates and MHCII−/− animals had minimal expression of lung Ciita at any time point after E. coli challenge.
source: As predicted from the enhanced numbers of MHCII-positive cells (Figure 2), the WT juvenile lungs had the highest fold increase in Ciita expression at 24 and 48 hr, PEC while the lungs from WT neonates and MHCII−/− animals had minimal expression of lung Ciita at any time point (Figure 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Lack of pathogen-induced Ciita expression in the lungs of WT neonatal and MHCII−/− mice is associated with lower numbers of IFNγ-producing CD4 T cells.
source: Studies have also demonstrated that a lack of pathogen-induced Ciita expression in the lungs of WT neonatal and MHCII−/− mice is associated with lower numbers of IFNγ-producing CD4 T cells (van den Elsen et al., 1998; Steimle et al., 1994; Chang et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to immunological studies.

claim: The transcription of IFN-inducible genes Cxcl10 and Ccl4 were minimal in response to E. coli challenge in WT neonatal and MHCII−/− animals.
source: In support of the idea that low Ciita expression might be linked to low IFNγ production, the transcription of IFN-inducible genes Cxcl10 were Ccl4 were minimal in response to E. coli challenge in WT neonatal and MHCII−/− animals (Figure 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Cxcl1 is a Th17-associated chemokine involved in neutrophil migration and NFkβ activation.
source: Cxcl1, a Th17-associated chemokine involved in neutrophil migration and NFkβ activation (Cai et al., 2010; Jin et al., 2014), and Ccl2(Mcp1), a monocyte chemoattractant induced by the NFkβ pathway (Bawazeer and Theoharides, 2019), were also upregulated in MHCII−/− juvenile lungs at 24 hr PEC (Figure 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to immunological studies.

claim: Ccl2(Mcp1) is a monocyte chemoattractant induced by the NFkβ pathway.
source: Cxcl1, a Th17-associated chemokine involved in neutrophil migration and NFkβ activation (Cai et al., 2010; Jin et al., 2014), and Ccl2(Mcp1), a monocyte chemoattractant induced by the NFkβ pathway (Bawazeer and Theoharides, 2019), were also upregulated in MHCII−/− juvenile lungs at 24 hr PEC (Figure 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to an immunological study.

claim: Cxcl1 and Ccl2 were upregulated in MHCII−/− juvenile lungs at 24 hr post-E. coli challenge.
source: Cxcl1, a Th17-associated chemokine involved in neutrophil migration and NFkβ activation (Cai et al., 2010; Jin et al., 2014), and Ccl2(Mcp1), a monocyte chemoattractant induced by the NFkβ pathway (Bawazeer and Theoharides, 2019), were also upregulated in MHCII−/− juvenile lungs at 24 hr PEC (Figure 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The fold changes in Ccl20 transcription post-E. coli challenge were substantially lower in WT juvenile lungs compared to WT neonates or MHCII−/− neonates and juveniles.
source: Interestingly, the fold changes in Ccl20 transcription, PEC were substantially lower in WT juvenile lungs compared to WT neonates or MHCII−/− neonates and juveniles.
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6.

claim: CCL20 has direct antibacterial properties.
source: In addition to its direct antibacterial properties (Starner et al., 2003), endothelial cell-derived CCL20 is reported to be chemotactic for CCR6+ lymphocytes and dendritic cells and to play key roles in innate and adaptive inflammation at barrier surfaces (Lee et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study on CCL20 function.

claim: Endothelial cell-derived CCL20 is chemotactic for CCR6+ lymphocytes and dendritic cells.
source: In addition to its direct antibacterial properties (Starner et al., 2003), endothelial cell-derived CCL20 is reported to be chemotactic for CCR6+ lymphocytes and dendritic cells and to play key roles in innate and adaptive inflammation at barrier surfaces (Lee et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study on CCL20 function.

claim: CCL20 plays key roles in innate and adaptive inflammation at barrier surfaces.
source: In addition to its direct antibacterial properties (Starner et al., 2003), endothelial cell-derived CCL20 is reported to be chemotactic for CCR6+ lymphocytes and dendritic cells and to play key roles in innate and adaptive inflammation at barrier surfaces (Lee et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study on CCL20 function.

claim: The early robust induction of Ccl20 in WT neonate and MHCII−/− lungs suggests a role for MHCII-mediated signaling in controlling the level of Ccl20 transcription.
source: The early robust induction of Ccl20 in WT neonate and MHCII−/− lungs suggests a role for MHCII-mediated signaling in controlling the level of Ccl20 transcription.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the qRT-PCR data showing differential Ccl20 expression patterns.

claim: Within 24 hr of post-E. coli challenge, there were significant reductions in both dendritic cells and alveolar macrophages that persisted in the neonatal lung.
source: Within 24 hr of PEC, there were significant reductions in both dendritic cells and alveolar macrophages that persisted in the neonatal lung but trended toward recovery to control levels by 72 hr PEC in the lungs from juveniles (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Dendritic cells and alveolar macrophages trended toward recovery to control levels by 72 hr post-E. coli challenge in juvenile lungs.
source: Within 24 hr of PEC, there were significant reductions in both dendritic cells and alveolar macrophages that persisted in the neonatal lung but trended toward recovery to control levels by 72 hr PEC in the lungs from juveniles (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Conventional dendritic cells are a prominent cell population during the first weeks of life in mouse lungs.
source: Conventional dendritic cells are a prominent cell population during the first weeks of life in the mouse lungs that exhibit an activation profile that differs from adult-derived lung DCs by being strong inducers of Th2 immune responses (Gollwitzer et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a developmental immunology study.

claim: Neonatal lung dendritic cells exhibit an activation profile that differs from adult-derived lung DCs by being strong inducers of Th2 immune responses.
source: Conventional dendritic cells are a prominent cell population during the first weeks of life in the mouse lungs that exhibit an activation profile that differs from adult-derived lung DCs by being strong inducers of Th2 immune responses (Gollwitzer et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a developmental immunology study.

claim: Colonization by the microbiota induces PD-L1 on neonatal lung dendritic cells.
source: Colonization by the microbiota induces PD-L1 (programmed cell-death ligand 1) on neonatal lung dendritic cells, which endows them with the capacity to induce regulatory T cells (Gollwitzer et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study on microbiota-immune interactions.

claim: PD-L1 expression on neonatal lung dendritic cells endows them with the capacity to induce regulatory T cells.
source: Colonization by the microbiota induces PD-L1 (programmed cell-death ligand 1) on neonatal lung dendritic cells, which endows them with the capacity to induce regulatory T cells (Gollwitzer et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study on microbiota-immune interactions.

claim: Alveolar macrophages reside in the bronchoalveolar space and alveoli.
source: Alveolar macrophages reside in the bronchoalveolar space and alveoli where these tissue resident cells function in regulating surfactant production, maintenance of epithelial barrier integrity, efferocytosis, and removal of inhaled particles (Bain and MacDonald, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review on lung macrophages.

claim: Alveolar macrophages function in regulating surfactant production, maintenance of epithelial barrier integrity, efferocytosis, and removal of inhaled particles.
source: Alveolar macrophages reside in the bronchoalveolar space and alveoli where these tissue resident cells function in regulating surfactant production, maintenance of epithelial barrier integrity, efferocytosis, and removal of inhaled particles (Bain and MacDonald, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review on lung macrophages.

claim: Recruited monocyte-derived macrophages are major contributors to innate defense against microbial exposure.
source: In addition, they have traditionally been designated as a first-line defense against air-borne pathogens, however, with the recent appreciation that recruited monocyte-derived macrophages are major contributors to the innate defense against microbial exposure, this aspect of alveolar macrophage function is under assessment (Aegerter et al., 2020; Liao et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent studies on macrophage function.

claim: Interstitial macrophages are located in the interstitial spaces between the alveoli and the capillaries as well as in the interstitial environment surrounding conducting airways.
source: The significantly less abundant interstitial macrophages are located in the interstitial spaces between the alveoli and the capillaries as well as in the interstitial environment surrounding conducting airways where they interact with stromal and other innate cells and play roles in inflammation (Chakarov et al., 2019; Schyns et al., 2019) and immunoregulation (Ural et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on interstitial macrophages.

claim: Interstitial macrophages interact with stromal and other innate cells and play roles in inflammation and immunoregulation.
source: The significantly less abundant interstitial macrophages are located in the interstitial spaces between the alveoli and the capillaries as well as in the interstitial environment surrounding conducting airways where they interact with stromal and other innate cells and play roles in inflammation (Chakarov et al., 2019; Schyns et al., 2019) and immunoregulation (Ural et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on interstitial macrophages.

claim: There was a significant reduction of alveolar macrophages at 24 hr post-E. coli challenge that persisted in neonatal lungs but was only transient in juvenile lungs.
source: As noted, there was a significant reduction of alveolar macrophages at 24 hr PEC that persisted in neonatal lungs but was only transient in juvenile lungs (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Acute loss of tissue resident macrophages at the early stages of inflammation is referred to as 'macrophage disappearance reaction'.
source: Acute loss of tissue resident macrophages at the early stages of inflammation, an occurrence referred to as 'macrophage disappearance reaction', has been described for peritoneal macrophages (Barth et al., 1995; Louwe et al., 2021) and in the lungs after LPS or CpG DNA challenge (Bain and MacDonald, 2022; Sabatel et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on macrophage dynamics.

claim: The transient loss of alveolar macrophages after LPS or CpG DNA challenge was accompanied by an expansion of interstitial macrophages.
source: Interestingly, in these studies the transient loss of alveolar macrophages was accompanied by an expansion of interstitial macrophages (Bain and MacDonald, 2022; Sabatel et al., 2017), similar to that seen in the lungs of WT juveniles challenged with live E. coli (Figures 2 and 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies and comparison with data in Figures 2 and 5.

claim: At steady state, interstitial macrophages are maintained through slow replacement by monocytes that take up residency in the lungs.
source: Current evidence indicates that at steady state, interstitial macrophages are maintained through slow replacement by monocytes that take up residency in the lungs (Chakarov et al., 2019; Schyns et al., 2019) and that a majority of the increase observed during inflammation is due to monocyte recruitment from the peripheral circulation (Huang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on macrophage homeostasis.

claim: A majority of the increase in interstitial macrophages observed during inflammation is due to monocyte recruitment from the peripheral circulation.
source: Current evidence indicates that at steady state, interstitial macrophages are maintained through slow replacement by monocytes that take up residency in the lungs (Chakarov et al., 2019; Schyns et al., 2019) and that a majority of the increase observed during inflammation is due to monocyte recruitment from the peripheral circulation (Huang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study on macrophage dynamics during inflammation.

claim: A majority of the increases in interstitial macrophages in juvenile lungs were made up of MHCIIhi cells.
source: A majority of the increases in interstitial macrophages in juvenile lungs were made up of MHCIIhi cells (data not shown) which supports the idea that they were derived from recruited monocytes (Chakarov et al., 2019; Schyns et al., 2019) and could provide a cellular context for the increased Ciita expression observed in the whole lungs from juveniles.
evidence: This claim is based on unpublished data mentioned in the text and supported by citations.

claim: The MHCIIhi interstitial macrophages in juvenile lungs were derived from recruited monocytes.
